2020-2021 Online Catalog URI 2020-2021 Online Catalog Film/Media Part of the Harrington School of Communication and Media (uri.edu/harrington), the Film/Media Program offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree and a minor. Faculty: Rebecca Romanow, Director. Professors Healey-Jamiel, Mandel, Moore, Sama, Swift, Trimm, and Walton; Associate Professors Chadha, Echevarría, Kealhofer-Kemp, Reyes, and Wyatt; Assistant Professor Jaacks; Adjunct Assistant Professors Bergstrom, and Zorabedian; Teaching Professors Brown and Romanow; Lecturer Corsano. The Major. Film/Media is an interdisciplinary program offering hands-on experience in documentary, experimental, narrative, and new media production, balanced with an emphasis on international cinemas, film/media history, criticism, and theory. Our curriculum reflects the dynamic and diverse nature of this field, approached from a perspective of film history and media theory. Students learn to work with the evolving and overlapping technologies involved in the production of moving images (including film, digital video, 3D animation, game design, and new media), with an understanding of the broadening and globalization of their cultural and aesthetic contexts. A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images. The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent

filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495; a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major (following).
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.
Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.

Production and Technique: These courses focus on the different approaches to and practices of film/video production—how moving images are created, designed, and used to serve a variety of functions: ART 105, 204, 213, 214, 215, 304, 306, 314, 315, 316; COM 306, 316B, 341, 342, 406, 410, 445; FLM 110, 220, 225, 230, 306, 351, 406, 445, 477, 491; JOR 221, 331.
Critical Studies: These courses emphasize the important traditions of genre and the literary and aesthetic approaches toward understanding and valuing film/media, and integrates them into their broad historical, cultural, and ideological contexts: AAF 352; ART 374, 376, 377; CLS 451; COM 346, 414; ENG 205 D, 245, 300A, 300B, 302, 303, 304, 305D, 352, 451; FLM 203, 204, 205, 206, 214, 352, 444, 451, 491, 495; FRN 320; GWS 350; HIS 358; HPR 344, 411; ITL 315; JOR 311; SPA 320; THE 182.
FRN 320, ITL 315, and SPA 320 are

taught in English. Other courses may be used for this category with prior approval of the program director. The following topics courses have been pre-approved: HPR 344 Images of Masculinity in Films, HPR 344 Rebel Images in Films, HPR 411 Film and Video Practicum, and GWS 350 Women and Film. Other film-based courses may count toward the major or the minor with the permission of the film/media program director. In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, students must complete a minimum of 24 credits and have a GPA of 2.00 or higher. A total of 120 credits is required for graduation. At least 42 of these must be in courses numbered 300 or above. The Minor. In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in film/media must complete 18 credit hours (at least 12 at the 200-level or higher) from those courses currently eligible to count toward the major. Courses in general education may count toward the minor. All courses must be taken for a grade except for the internship (Field Experience). It is strongly suggested that at least one course in the minor be from each of the following two approaches to film and media study: Production. These courses focus on the practices of film/video/media production, the design and creation of moving images. Criticism. These courses address critical and theoretical approaches to film/media and the broader contexts of international film history, genre, and ideology in which they are situated. It is well-suited for students whose career goals call for training in more than one discipline or who want a breadth of knowledge in several fields rather than a depth of knowledge in a single discipline.
With this degree, one can be even more directly educated with regard to several, specific, job-relevant studies.
This interdisciplinary “three-minor’ major also may work well for students who do not want to limit their career options by majoring in just one area of study.
For the purposes of this proposal, the word “minor" is used to refer to coursework associated with recognized areas of study (as minors) at the University of Rhode Island.
Specifically, students will complete an application that proposes one thematic or topical concentration made up of three (3) recognized minor areas of study that will not be restricted

to conventional departmental or unit boundaries.
The application must include a statement of rationale for the combination of areas of study.
The application then must be reviewed and approved by the Director of School of Professional and Continuing Studies (or designee).
Students seeking this program must declare it as their major in the same manner, and at the same time,that other URI students declare a major.
It is important to note that, through the completion of this program, students will not receive minors in the three areas of study, rather the integrated coursework will be used to fulfill the requirements of the interdisciplinary major.
Upon completion of the program, the student's approved interdisciplinary concentration will be noted on the university transcript.
Moreover, the Learner Designed major provides an opportunity to develop and pursue a course of study centered on a unifying theme, problem, or issue.
Students earning a degree in Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies, Learner Designed major will: · Possess an interdisciplinary perspective by integrating knowledge and skills from three areas of study.

Communicate meaningful connections effectively across disciplinary boundaries.
The Learner Designed major will include: (a) URI General Education Requirements; (b) Minor Area of Study 1 (18- 24 credits), Minor Area of Study 2 (18 -24 credits), and Minor Area of Study 3 (18 -24 credits); (c) BIS 100, 399, ITR 302, 304; and, (d) elective courses totaling 120 credit hours.
The capstone experience (BIS 399) provides a structure that enables the student to integrate knowledge and skills from coursework and related experiences with a research project.
The project must be designed so that it allows the student to demonstrate the integration of subject matter, theory, and practice.
Students are required to meet with the Director of School of Professional & Continuing Studies (or designee) to plan a project proposal.
The Learner Designed major will provide students with a well-rounded education in multiple academic disciplines, allowing them to gain skills employers will find desirable, including critical thinking, communication and creative problem-solving.
Employers appreciate applicants with diverse backgrounds and the ability to integrate multiple viewpoints.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ALAN SHAWN FEINSTEIN COLLEGE OF EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES THINKBIG WEDO" SCHOOL OF PROFESSIONAL AND CONTINUING STUDIES Shepard Building,80Washington Street,Providence,RI2903SA 3/16/21 Dear Chris Kincaid and the Curriculum and Standards Committee, I write as a follow-up to our conversation (3/15/21) regarding the Interdisciplinary Studies Learner Designed (Three- Minor) Major proposal submitted by the School of Professional Studies.
Offered below are reflections and rationale for this innovative program.Thank youfor your review.
Sincerely, Jonathan Kroll Program Rationale: The Schoolof Professional Studies is motivated to provide relevant and resonant programs for S.T.A.R. (Service members, Transfer, Adult, and Returning) students.
The vast majority of these students are working full time while studying, caring for family, and serving their communities.
The Learner Designed Major (also referred to as the Three Minor Major)was crafted so that enrolled students can curate a program-of-study that will enable them to acquire knowledge and advance their professional pursuits.

Rather than force these students into traditional academic programs, this major degree combines three minors of the students own choosing,integrates their learning through specific interdisciplinary (BIS) courses, and fulfills General Education and elective credits to reinforce URI's commitment to a comprehensive learning experience.
Q1)What are thegoals and the purposes of students selecting the Three Minor Major?
S.T.A.R. students are unique in that their academic pursuits are directly connected to their professional status and objectives.
They are working full-time.
Many have been for years,if not decades.
The Three Minor Major is structured to maximize the connections between their professional stations and academic coursework.Rather than study in a traditional major program, the learner designed program enables students to immerse themselves in three academic areas-of-attention.For example,if one of our students is a Coordinator of a nonprofit community agency that focuses on food injustice for an elderly population, she might combine the Gerontology, Hunger Studies, and Leadership Studies minors to curate a highly specialized and resonant Major.

No single major degree would be as academically supportive to her current and future professional endeavors as this combination.
Similarly, if a student was the Chef/Owner of a sports bar, he might combine minors in Finance, Marketing, and Sports Mediaand Communication to center his studies on what matters most to him.No singular major can provide an academic course of study that is as preparatory for his particular academic needs and interests than the strategic combination of three minor degrees.
The University of Rhode Island is an equal opportunity employer commited to community equity and diversity and to the principles of a ff rm at ive action.

Q2) Do the minors need to be related or can a student use any 3 minors that the university offers?
Students enrolled in the Three Minor Major can include any three minors of their choosing.
This is intended to provide maximum flexibility while aiso ensuring the design of their major reflects each student's individualized academic and professional pursuits.
Q3) Is there a requirement of a specific number of 300-level courses?
No.
Students are not required to take a specific number of 300-level courses.
Q4) Can you give a quick summary of the program including how the student will be advised?
When students enroll in the Learner Designed Major, they will meet with both their Academic Advisor as well as the School of Professional Studies’ Director.
These initial conversations are intended to lay a foundation and ensure that the students have both the discipline and a clarity of what is expected as Three Minor Major students.
These students will also enroll in BIS 199, the program's introductory course.
Here, they will explore critical approaches to interdisciplinary thinking and begin reflecting on which minors will support their pursuits.

As students continue through their program, they will meet regularly with their Academic Advisor to ensure their course selections strategically align with their intended three minors as well as other requisite courses (i.e., General Education).
Following the completion of at least two courses in each minor, they will enroll in BIs 299a two-credit course designed to assist these students in intentionally integrating their learning. (Students’ Advising conversations will illuminate the desire that this program is intended to be interdisciplinary and that each semester they should be registering for courses in multiple disciplines, rather than attempting to complete one minor one before the others.) Similar to the BIS 199, the BIS 299 course will be taught by a core faculty member within the School of Professional Studies.
Further advising by their formal Academic Advisor and faculty members, will enable these students to strategically select courses that fulfill minor, general education, and elective credits-—-rather than random courses that do not lead to degree fulfillment.
The program concludes with BIS 399: Supervised Senior Project.

With this course, students will be expected to purposefully integrate their multi-discipline learning in a culminating academic project. (This course will also be taught by a core faculty member from the School of Professional Studies.) Similar to all School of Professional Studies students, these Learner Designed Major students will engage in tailored advising conversations throughout their URI experience.
More so, as an intimate community, Academic Advisors, Administrators, and Faculty are constantly engaging with one another as well as in advisory dialogue with students to best be of support, serve as guides, and maximize adult-learner best-practices.
We expect this to continue when the Three Minor Major degree is approved and ultimately launches. 2
